findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Worthing Capital Investment Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 v2
findings.headline: Heat Network investment of £19.6m represents significant debt-funded capital commitment
findings.detail: The council is committing £19.6m to Heat Network projects over four years (Enabling Works £5.7m, Carbon Neutral 2030 £5.7m, Splashpoint/Pavilion connections £8.7m). Of this, £7.2m is funded through prudential borrowing rather than grants, making it a substantial long-term debt-funded obligation tied to a specific decarbonisation strategy.
findings.matters: A £19.6m capital commitment to a single strategic initiative, with nearly £7m financed by council borrowing, concentrates capital risk on the success of one programme and increases the debt service burden if returns (e.g. heat sales revenue) do not materialise.
findings.figures: Heat Network Enabling Works £4.2m; Carbon Neutral 2030 scheme £5.7m; Heat Network Splashpoint/connections £8.7m. Total borrowing for Heat Network: ~£7.2m
findings.quote: Worthing Heat Network Enabling Works 4,161,136 | 9,666,553 and Carbon Neutral 2030 : Worthing Heat Network 5,659,993 | 5,009,016 | - | 650,977

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Worthing Capital Investment Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 v2
findings.headline: Cycle Lane scheme funding explicitly dependent on CIL receipts with no alternative funding source
findings.detail: The £2m Cycle Lane (George V to Sea Lane) project is marked as conditional: 'Subject to CIL funding being available'. CIL receipts for future years (2026/27-2028/29) drop sharply to £100-£280k against £6.3m in 2025/26, meaning this and other schemes cannot proceed without securing external contributions.
findings.matters: A £2m capital scheme with contingent funding represents execution risk; if CIL receipts do not materialise as planned, the council either postpones the work or must find alternative financing, potentially increasing borrowing.
findings.figures: Cycle Lane budget £2,000,000; S106/CIL expected to fall from £6.3m (2025/26) to £280k (2026/27)
findings.quote: (Cycle Lane - George V to Sea Lane.  Subject to CIL funding being available) 2,000,000 2,000,000

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Worthing Capital Investment Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 v2
findings.headline: Montague Place Improvements repriced from £400k to £3m within the same financial year
findings.detail: The design works for Montague Place public realm improvements increased from a draft estimate of £400,000 to a current estimate of £3,000,041 — a 650% repricing. The document provides no explanation for this substantial movement in the same year.
findings.matters: A sevenfold increase in a single scheme's cost within months suggests either significant scope creep, cost inflation that could affect other projects, or an initial estimate that was unreliably preliminary.
findings.figures: Draft Original: £400,000; Current Estimate: £3,000,041
findings.quote: Montague Place Improvements - Design works 558936 FB 3,300,000 299,959 400,000 3,000,041

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Worthing Capital Investment Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29 v2
findings.headline: Prudential borrowing requirement for 2025/26 nearly doubled from draft estimate
findings.detail: The current capital programme requires £25m in prudential borrowing for 2025/26, compared to the draft estimate of £13.2m — an increase of £11.8m or 89%. Total borrowing across the four-year programme is £37.8m, with peak interest costs of £423,376 in 2027/28.
findings.matters: A material increase in planned borrowing raises questions about whether the council's original financial assumptions have changed and what this means for future revenue budgets and debt service capacity.
findings.figures: Draft £13,233,507; Current £25,002,603; Interest costs peak at £423,376 (2027/28)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Adur Capital Investment Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Major Repairs Reserve drops from £4.8m to £2.3m by 2028/29, constraining future capital flexibility
findings.detail: Reserve funding for housing capital investment rises to £4.8m in 2026/27 then falls sharply to £2.3m by 2028/29 — a £2.5m reduction. This pattern suggests reserves are being drawn down rather than accumulated for future capital needs.
findings.matters: Depleting reserves reduce the council's ability to fund emergencies or new capital schemes without increasing borrowing. It also signals the current capital plan is consuming accumulated reserves, which cannot be repeated indefinitely.
findings.quote: Major Repairs Reserve (Adur Homes Capital Investment Programme) 3,500,000     3,500,000     3,500,000      4,809,328     2,299,740     122,500        158,227     77,961

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Adur Capital Investment Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29
findings.headline: £22.5m responsive capital repairs programme signals maintenance backlog in housing stock
findings.detail: Adur Homes faces £22.5m in responsive repairs across the period, described as 'Urgent capital repairs identified in advance of planned capital works,' with £2.5m allocated to 2025/26 alone. This is the largest unscheduled repair line in the housing capital budget.
findings.matters: A large backlog of urgent repairs suggests prior underinvestment or asset condition deterioration in the council's housing stock, which increases risk of accelerating maintenance costs and asset degradation if the backlog is not cleared.
findings.quote: Responsive Capital Repairs 118525 DE 22,480,000     2,500,000     2,500,000      2,394,300       8,685,700     8,900,000 … Urgent capital repairs identified in advance of planned capital works

findings.paper_title: Appendix 2 Adur Capital Investment Programme 2025-26 to 2028-29
findings.headline: Prudential borrowing spikes to £27.5m in 2026/27 — a 141% increase from the prior year
findings.detail: Borrowing rises sharply from £11.4m in 2025/26 to £27.5m in 2026/27, then moderates to £8.9m and £6.6m in the following two years. This volatility is unexplained in the document itself and creates material revenue budget impacts.
findings.matters: The scale and unexplained nature of the borrowing spike is a material change in the council's capital strategy that lenders assess for sustainability; the spike also commits future revenue to debt service costs (interest charges £431k–£324k annually).

findings.headline: Worthing General Fund Working Balance at 8% of budget (lower end of 6-10% policy) with £1.464m drawn from reserves in 2025/26; Adur reserves described as 'very low'
findings.detail: Worthing's General Fund Working Balance is £1,976,431 (8% of budget), at the lower end of the council's established 6-10% policy. The council transferred £1.464m into reserves during 2025/26 but the paper notes the financial strategy aimed to rebuild reserves—a task that 'can only[...] a risk which [...] report.' Adur's overall reserves are described as 'very low' despite recent contributions.
findings.matters: Low reserve buffers constrain a council's ability to absorb shocks (e.g. further homelessness demand spikes, income slippages). At 8%, Worthing has minimal headroom; any further deterioration would exhaust reserves and trigger insolvency.
findings.figures: Worthing General Fund Working Balance £1,976,431 (8% of budget), transfers to reserves £1,463,888, Adur reserves 'very low'
findings.quote: The Council's established policy is to maintain the General Fund Working Balance at [...] between 6% and 10% of [...] The current balance is £1,976,431. This balance represents 8% of [...] It should be noted that the overall level of reserves held is very low and the importance[...]

findings.headline: Adur Housing Revenue Account overspent by £1.167m and HRA reserves fell to £0.693m (from £1.704m budgeted) driven by void losses and disrepair liability
findings.detail: The ring-fenced HRA overspent by £1.167m. Key drivers: £705k void property rent loss (stock not generating income), £1.31m repairs and maintenance additional costs, and £310k legal fees for housing disrepair claims. HRA General Reserve fell from £1.22m to £409k, reducing financial buffer for a ring-fenced account managing 11,000+ properties.
findings.matters: HRA deficits and void loss signal aging stock and rising maintenance liability. Disrepair claims represent latent legal/financial exposure. Reserve depletion in a ring-fenced account limits future flexibility for capital investment or emergency repairs.
findings.figures: £1.167m HRA overspend, £705k void loss, £1.31m maintenance overspend, £310k disrepair legal fees, HRA reserves £0.693m (down from £1.704m), General Reserve £409k (down from £1.22m)
findings.quote: The HRA over spend against the budget for 2025/26 is £1.167m. The most significant[...] due to: ● Void property rent loss (including losses in associated service charges and[...] - £705k adverse. ● Repairs and maintenance additional costs - £1.31m adverse. ● Legal fees for advice and settlement of costs in relation to housing disrepair claims[...]

findings.headline: Worthing bereavement services income collapsed by £647k against budget target; crematorium delivered £749k shortfall
findings.detail: The crematorium delivered £749k shortfall against service budgets despite the council investing in the facility. Income continues to face pressure as funeral directors increasingly invest in developing their own chapels, and there is a rise in direct cremations (lower margin) at the expense of attended funerals. The council had budgeted for higher-margin income streams but market behaviour shifted.
findings.matters: A council service with capital investment is generating a 22% budget miss, suggesting either poor asset management or diminishing market for council facilities; indicates capital deployment risk.
findings.figures: £647k service deficit against budget, crematorium £749k shortfall, cemetery income overachieved by £68k
findings.quote: Worthing crematorium delivered a £749k shortfall against the service budgets. Income continues [...] to invest in [...] additional £80 per [...] against budget, and [...] exceeded budget by £28k.

findings.headline: Worthing car parks income shortfall of £674k and Grafton MSCP closure creating operational capacity loss
findings.detail: Worthing car parks underachieved against budget by £918k overspend, driven by £674k income shortfall plus £237k overspend in Multi-Storey Car Park maintenance. The Grafton MSCP closure is cited as a reason for both income loss and elevated maintenance costs for reactive repairs. Parking is a key revenue stream; its decline signals either demand weakness or operational issues.
findings.matters: Car parks are a major discretionary revenue source; significant underperformance indicates demand weakness in the town centre or operational failures in a managed asset.
findings.figures: £918k car parks overspend, £674k income shortfall, £237k MSCP overspend
findings.quote: Worthing Car Parks underachieved against the budget due [...] of £674K to the income budget, as [...] a £237K overspend in [...] MSCP.

findings.headline: Worthing's homelessness overspend of £3,402k driven by government grant underfunding and 221% growth in exempt accommodation units since 2021
findings.detail: Homelessness costs overspent by £3,402k in Worthing. The paper states grant funding is insufficient: Worthing receives £1,175 per household in prevention grant compared to the national average of £4,917 per claim (a shortfall of £3,742 per claim). Since 2021 there has been a 221% increase in exempt accommodation units in Worthing. The statutory duty to house homeless persons is not adequately funded by central government, creating structural budget pressure.
findings.matters: Homelessness is a statutory duty but government grant is insufficient and volatile. The 221% growth in exempt accommodation indicates continued expansion of liability; lenders need to understand this is non-discretionary, underfunded expenditure with no clear ceiling.
findings.figures: £3,402k overspend, £1,175 grant per household vs £4,917 average, 221% increase in exempt units since 2021, Worthing variation to average -£3,742
findings.quote: The final year outturn for 2025/26 for Adur is an £893k overspend and for Worthing is an £3,402k overspend. Cost pressures continue to persist in discharging our statutory duties due to the[...] significant pressure arises [...] Since 2021 there has been a 221% increase in units in Worthing.

findings.headline: Worthing required £3.785m Exceptional Funding Support from government to balance its 2025/26 budget after a 21% operational overspend
findings.detail: Worthing's operational overspend reached £3,785k (21% of budget), with significant in-year spend controls and savings processes implemented to mitigate an even larger projected overspend identified earlier in the year. The council could not absorb this within normal budget management and required exceptional government funding to balance the accounts. This is the clearest indicator of financial distress requiring external bailout.
findings.matters: A council requiring exceptional government funding has exhausted normal financial management options and signals serious solvency stress; lenders need to understand structural deficits and operational control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £3,785k overspend, 21% of operational budget, exceptional funding requirement £3,785k
findings.quote: The final position for operational services was an underspend for Adur District Council of £325k and an overspend in Worthing Borough Council of £3,785k. This represents a 3% underspend against the budget for Adur and 21% overspend in Worthing.

findings.headline: Bereavement service income is below budget with uncertain recovery, as post-pandemic death rates remain lower than pre-pandemic levels.
findings.detail: The councils undertook an external bereavement service review and reset income assumptions for Worthing in the 2026/27 budget 'to address the changing market demand away from full cremations to direct only.' However, 'the service income is still currently below budget and there is a risk that the assumed growth in new memorial income does not close this shortfall.' The underlying cause is that death rates 'continue to be lower following the pandemic,' and this is a demand driver entirely outside the council's control.
findings.matters: An income stream the council is relying on to improve is both underperforming its budget and dependent on execution of new 'memorial income work streams' with uncertain takeup. Underlying demand (death rate) remains below pre-pandemic levels.
findings.figures: Service income described as 'still currently below budget.' Income reset was completed but still not delivering target.
findings.quote: The service income is still currently below budget and there is a risk that the assumed growth in new memorial income does not close this shortfall. The shortfall is largely linked to the death rate which continues to be lower following the pandemic.

findings.headline: Councils missed the Environment Act statutory deadline of March 2026 for food waste collection rollout; implementation now expected Autumn 2026.
findings.detail: The Environment Act required councils to implement food waste collections by March 2026. The councils have failed to meet this deadline: 'As a result of the delay in certainty regarding funding and due to the high demand for food waste vehicles (lead times are over 12 months) the councils were unable to meet the deadline for the roll out of the service, which is expected to be Autumn 2026, rather than April 2026.' The revenue funding allocation 'was only announced in December 2025' and cannot be clearly identified within the overall settlement, creating ongoing uncertainty about true costs.
findings.matters: Statutory deadline failure suggests delivery or planning weakness. Revenue funding for an ongoing statutory service is still unidentified and rolled into general formula funding, creating budget uncertainty.
findings.figures: Deadline was March/April 2026; new target Autumn 2026 (6+ months late). Vehicle lead times 'over 12 months.'
findings.quote: As a result of the delay in certainty regarding funding and due to the high demand for food waste vehicles (lead times are over 12 months) the councils were unable to meet the deadline for the roll out of the service, which is expected to be Autumn 2026, rather than April 2026.

findings.headline: Worthing's major car parks (Grafton MSCP and Union Place NCP) are closed for redevelopment; remaining assets are deteriorating because maintenance is unaffordable.
findings.detail: Grafton Multi Storey Car Park 'has closed pending redevelopment' and Union Place NCP 'has closed and this site is being redeveloped.' High Street MSCP 'does require investment to maintain its structural integrity, install edge protection, improve the aesthetics' but 'the deterioration in the council's financial position means that this is not a viable option.' Worthing parking income 'has not recovered since the pandemic,' and the paper warns of rising EV use and weighloading concerns. Meanwhile parking income continues to perform well in Adur (surface car parks, lower maintenance).
findings.matters: Major income-generating assets are offline with uncertain reopening, and necessary maintenance is being deferred due to budget constraints. This creates ongoing income risk and potential asset deterioration liability.
findings.figures: Parking described as 'greater financial risk in Worthing compared to Adur.' High Street MSCP investment 'is not a viable option.'
findings.quote: Grafton Multi Storey Car Park (MSCP) has closed pending redevelopment, and the former NCP car park in Union Place has closed and this site is being redeveloped.

findings.headline: Exempt supported accommodation (unregistered, uncontrolled rent levels) is driving the core housing cost problem that central funding does not cover.
findings.detail: Worthing has a 'high level of Exempt Supported Accommodation in the area operated by unregistered providers, where the usual limits on rent levels do not apply.' The paper explains: 'At present, the additional housing costs that are charged are not covered by the government through housing benefit and currently have to be met by the borough council, creating a major pressure on Worthing council finances.' Historically a ring-fenced 'Supporting People' programme was de-ringfenced in 2009 and rolled into the county grant in 2011, removing dedicated funding. The council is working to transition to registered providers only, but 'it will take some years to achieve.'
findings.matters: This is a structural cost driver the council cannot control—rents are set by unregistered private landlords and are not capped like mainstream housing benefit. Government has acknowledged the funding formula is 'out of date' but new allocations 'did not fully mitigate the financial pressures from the increased demand.'
findings.figures: No single figure, but described alongside temporary accommodation as one of the 'two major cost pressures' now 'leading to the expected ongoing need for exceptional funding support.'
findings.quote: At present, the additional housing costs that are charged are not covered by the government through housing benefit and currently have to be met by the borough council, creating a major pressure on Worthing council finances.

findings.headline: Worthing holds only 6.1% working balance reserves at the absolute minimum policy level, with no buffer for unexpected costs.
findings.detail: Worthing's working balance stands at £1,976k against a budget of £24,655k (6.1%), meeting only the minimum policy threshold. Total revenue reserves including earmarked amounts are just 10% of budget, compared to Adur's 50%. The paper warns: 'Worthing in particular holds a very low level of reserves which leaves it in a vulnerable position to financially mitigate any volatile or unbudgeted pressures.' Proposed annual reserve rebuilding of £100-500k is very slow given the volatility described.
findings.matters: Lenders assess reserve levels as a shock absorber. At 6.1% (minimum policy level), any unbudgeted pressure or income shortfall forces immediate additional borrowing. The paper itself notes the councils will have to 'manage a very tight set of finances and considerable risk for the next few years.'
findings.figures: Working balance £1,976k (6.1% of budget). Total reserves £4,981k (10% of budget). Rebuild provision: £100-500k annually.
findings.quote: Worthing in particular holds a very low level of reserves which leaves it in a vulnerable position to financially mitigate any volatile or unbudgeted pressures.

findings.headline: Worthing requires ongoing exceptional government funding to balance its budget because central funding does not cover housing costs.
findings.detail: Worthing has received exceptional funding support in 2025/26 and 2026/27, and the paper explicitly states it is 'assumed that a similar request for support will be made to enable the council to set a balanced budget for 27/28.' The cumulative budget shortfall grows from £4.7m in 2027/28 to £10.1m by 2031/32. This is not a temporary issue but a structural problem: 'underlying funding formula issues mean that central funding continues to be insufficient to bridge the financial gap.'
findings.matters: A council dependent on exceptional government funding is a lending risk—it signals structural financial problems rather than short-term pressures, and exceptional funding cannot be banked on to solve permanent structural issues.
findings.figures: Cumulative shortfall 2027/28: £4,672k; 2031/32: £10,080k. EFS borrowing cost 2027/28: £468k, rising to £1,009k by 2031/32.
findings.quote: It is expected that exceptional funding support will again be needed for Worthing whilst underlying funding formula issues mean that central funding continues to be insufficient to bridge the financial gap.

findings.headline: Council generated £6.8m in capital receipts from asset sales in 2025/26, including major Worthing property sales
findings.detail: Worthing sold Union Place (£4.1m) and Beta Building (£2.7m). Adur received £2.1m from housing Right to Buy sales. These receipts are now held as capital resources. The size of one-off asset sales raises questions about revenue generation sustainability.
findings.matters: Large property sales fund capital programmes but are not recurring; lenders assess whether councils depend on one-off asset sales rather than sustainable revenue or grant funding.
findings.figures: Worthing Union Place sale £4.1m; Beta Building £2.7m; Adur RTB receipts £2.1m
findings.quote: Sale of Union Place 4,109,000; Sale of Beta Building 2,708,333

findings.headline: Capital programme delivery significantly underperformed budgets: Adur spent £14.6m of £36.8m (39%), Worthing spent £21.1m of £35.2m (60%)
findings.detail: Both councils budgeted for substantially more capital spending than they delivered. While much is carried forward to 2026/27, the scale of carry-forward (£12.1m for Adur, £15.0m for Worthing) suggests planning or delivery issues, with projects delayed a year or more.
findings.matters: Persistent underspends on capital programmes flag either optimistic budgeting, delivery capability issues, or project viability problems; lenders assess whether the council can execute capital strategies efficiently.
findings.figures: Adur: budget £36.8m, spend £14.6m, underspend £22.2m. Worthing: budget £35.2m, spend £21.1m, underspend £14.1m
findings.quote: Actual expenditure for the year amounted to £14,551,052, resulting in a variance of £22,211,547 from the current estimate

findings.headline: Worthing's Disabled Facilities Grant programme overspent by £598k as mandatory grants exceeded budget allocation
findings.detail: The budget was set at £1.515m but actual expenditure reached £2.113m. While funded by the Better Care Fund, this represents demand exceeding the council's initial allocation and signals higher-than-forecast need for adaptations.
findings.matters: Overspends on mandatory services indicate either poor demand forecasting or deteriorating housing stock condition; both flag financial management or service delivery risk.
findings.figures: Budget £1.515m; actual spend £2.113m; overspend £598,326
findings.quote: These grants are mandatory and the Council has to approve all eligible grants. All approvals are for 12 months and works can be undertaken at any time in this period. The Council has received sufficient Better Care Grant to fund all 2025/26 expenditure

findings.headline: Albion Street Housing development for 49 social homes has encountered several issues
findings.detail: The HRA project has experienced problems beyond design, with an overspend of £127k against budget. The paper indicates these issues are unresolved ('current status' suggests ongoing problems extending into 2026/27).
findings.matters: Housing delivery and cost control are key council capabilities that lenders monitor; project delays and overspends on social housing signal delivery and financial management risk.
findings.figures: Overspend £127k
findings.quote: The project to deliver 49 social housing properties has encountered several issues

findings.headline: Worthing Integrated Care Centre overspend of £1.95m requires ongoing expenditure for occupancy standards
findings.detail: The project had a revised estimate of £585,919 but actual outturn reached £2,535,876. The paper notes practical completion occurred in December 2024, but substantial additional expenditure is still needed to meet standards necessary for occupancy. This signals ongoing cost pressures and project complications.
findings.matters: A material project overspend represents cost control failure and flagged ongoing spend commitments; lenders assess whether the council can deliver major capital schemes on budget.
findings.figures: Revised estimate £585,919; actual outturn £2,535,876; overspend £1,949,957
findings.quote: Practical completion in December 2024 however expenditure is required to meet standards necessary for occupancy

findings.headline: Worthing is using capital receipts to fund Local Government Reorganisation transition and ongoing transformation
findings.detail: Cabinet approved use of capital receipts to fund both residual transformation costs from an Organisational Design Programme and Local Government Reorganisation transition work. No figures or timeline are provided.
findings.matters: Local Government Reorganisation is significant structural change affecting operations and staffing. Using capital receipts for it suggests material costs and raises sustainability questions if the work extends beyond one-off transition.
findings.figures: No figures provided for reorganisation or transformation costs
findings.quote: the use of Capital receipts be approved to support a. Residual transformation costs associated with the Organisational Design Programme; and b. Transition work required for the Local Government Reorganisation

findings.headline: Worthing's 2026/27 budget depends on an Exceptional Funding Request to government
findings.detail: Cabinet acknowledged progress on an Exceptional Funding Request and recommended a net budget requirement of £24,655,120 to Full Council. No detail on the EFR's amount, reason, or approval status is provided in this extract.
findings.matters: Exceptional Funding Requests indicate the council cannot balance its budget from normal government grant and local resources. If the request fails, the council faces a significant funding gap.
findings.figures: £24,655,120 net budget requirement
findings.quote: progress with the Exceptional Funding Request be acknowledged and it be recommended to Full Council that the draft budgets for 2026/27 at Appendix 7 and the transfer to reserves leading to a net budget requirement of £24,655,120

findings.headline: The council is proposing a 2.97% council tax increase to maintain frontline services amid extremely challenging financial circumstances
findings.detail: The council frames the council tax increase as 'a necessary step to protect services and maintain stability in extremely challenging circumstances'. The increase is justified by structural budget pressures affecting councils across the country and the need to support vulnerable residents, indicating the revenue budget cannot support existing service levels without additional income.
findings.matters: Council tax increases necessary to maintain existing service levels rather than fund growth signal fundamental structural revenue pressure that may constrain future flexibility.
findings.figures: 2.97% increase in Borough Council's share
findings.quote: To maintain frontline services and continue supporting our most vulnerable residents, we are proposing a 2.97% increase in the Borough Council's share of Council Tax.

findings.headline: The council has requested Exceptional Support Funding from MHCLG again, indicating a pattern of structural financial difficulty requiring government intervention
findings.detail: The council states it 'requested Exceptional Support Funding once again'—the word 'again' indicating this is not a first-time request but a repeat. The speech notes local government has 'endured decades of unsustainable funding reductions', and this exceptional funding is described as reflecting 'the scale of the pressures we face', yet is presented as evidence of responsible financial management.
findings.matters: Repeated reliance on exceptional government support indicates the council has underlying structural budget difficulties that cannot be solved through normal management, discipline, or prudent borrowing limits alone.
findings.figures: funding requested repeatedly
findings.quote: we requested Exceptional Support Funding once again - and I am pleased to confirm that our request has been successful.

findings.headline: Housing demand is consuming over one-third of the council budget and continues to exceed targets, creating sustained financial pressure through 2026
findings.detail: The council identifies homelessness and housing need as one of its most serious challenges. Over a third of the total council budget is now spent addressing housing demand. Despite efforts to deliver more affordable homes, demand continues to exceed the targets set, placing sustained pressure on finances into 2026 and beyond.
findings.matters: Demand-driven spending that exceeds targets is uncontrollable budget pressure—the council may be unable to balance budgets without cutting services elsewhere or further tax increases.
findings.figures: a third of council budget
findings.quote: But demand continues to exceed targets set, placing sustained pressure on our finances into 2026 and beyond.

findings.headline: The council inherited a £30m-plus Worthing Integrated Care Centre project with escalating contractor issues and financial risk to taxpayers
findings.detail: When the current administration took office, a £30 million-plus financial liability was already underway from this project. Officers are devoting significant time to ongoing contractor issues, particularly with the water system. The council states this poses substantial financial risk because it is funding and delivering a building for the NHS rather than for itself, and acknowledges the risk has escalated since inception.
findings.matters: An inherited capital project with active contractor problems and escalating risk could require substantial draw-down of reserves, impact borrowing capacity, and divert resources from other priorities.
findings.figures: £30 million-plus financial liability
findings.quote: But it remains deeply regrettable that this council is funding and delivering a building for the NHS at such financial risk to local taxpayers. It was a risky project at inception - and the risk has only escalated.

findings.headline: Commercial property investment income relies on continued property market performance; governance changes limit this avenue
findings.detail: The council has generated £6.2m income from strategic property investment funds. However, the budget notes that the Prudential Code guidance 'effectively prohibits solely commercial investment' and the council is now required to 'review current commercial investments.' Future income cannot be assumed at historical levels.
findings.matters: For a council with minimal reserves and growing deficits, losing a £6.2m income stream would be catastrophic. New restrictions on commercial property investment reduce this option as a pressure valve for future deficits.
findings.figures: Current income generation £6.2m; restrictions on new commercial-only investment
findings.quote: guidance on commerciality which effectively prohibits solely commercial investment and [...] review current commercial investments.

findings.headline: Food Waste Service introduction adds £940k committed cost in 2026/27
findings.detail: Mandatory new food waste collection service starts in 2026/27 at a cost of £940k (growing to £970k-£1.070m in later years). This is a statutory obligation with no offsetting income, a fixed cost commitment the council cannot avoid.
findings.matters: This is a new statutory obligation that adds to the baseline cost structure. Once implemented, it becomes a permanent budget commitment that cannot be easily cut, reducing future flexibility.
findings.quote: Food Waste Service introduction 940

findings.headline: Council must increase council tax by 2.97% (near maximum 3% threshold) just to balance the budget
findings.detail: The budget model requires a 2.97% council tax increase. The government allows up to 3% without referendum. A lower increase would widen the deficit further; going above 3% requires a referendum the council cannot afford to lose. This leaves no room for a lower increase to ease taxpayer burden.
findings.matters: The council is at the maximum council tax level it can impose without a referendum. This removes a key lever for future budget balancing, forcing future gaps to be closed through service cuts or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Maximum allowed 3%; proposed 2.97%; generates £11.373m; at 2% would generate £11.265m (gap of £108k)
findings.quote: The executive will need to consider for recommendation to Full Council whether to increase council tax by the maximum level equating to 2.97% in 2026/27, or by a lower amount

findings.headline: £4m+ in savings to be delivered but delivery mechanisms not detailed for future years
findings.detail: The document states the council is 'delivering savings of over £4m' but the annual breakdown shows savings required of £1.381m (2027/28), £484k (2028/29), then £2.302m (2029/30) and £1.969m (2030/31). No specific proposals are outlined for these future-year savings, only that services have been 'reset' and contingencies removed.
findings.matters: Unidentified future savings are a red flag: councils often struggle to deliver savings when budget lines have been reset to minimal levels. If these savings do not materialise, the council will face new deficits.
findings.quote: Annual Savings to be found - (1,381) (484) 2,302 1,969 [for years 2027-2030]

findings.headline: Medium-term forecast shows cumulative shortfall growing to £6.878m by 2030/31 despite announced savings plans
findings.detail: The 5-year forecast shows the annual savings gap widening after an initial dip. By 2030/31, even with the planned annual savings being delivered, the council faces a cumulative shortfall of £6.878m. This indicates the savings identified (£4m+) are insufficient to resolve the underlying structural deficit.
findings.matters: A worsening medium-term outlook despite savings plans suggests either the savings are optimistic, the pressures are structural, or new revenue sources are needed. For a lender, this signals future difficulty.
findings.quote: Current projected cumulative shortfall [table showing]: 2026/27 £4,472k ... 2030/31 £6,878k

findings.headline: Business Rates Reset claws back £11.9m of council's accumulated growth since 2013
findings.detail: The Business Rates Retention Scheme reset (first change since 2013) pulls back the £11.9m of accumulated growth Worthing had built up. The council moves from a 'retained growth' position to paying a levy. This is a one-off hit in 2026/27 with Baseline Funding increasing from £2.941m (2025/26) to £4.281m, but growth assumptions are zero.
findings.matters: This removes a major income source that the council had relied on during earlier budget pressures. The reset effectively redistributes local growth nationally, reducing Worthing's income flexibility in future years.
findings.figures: £11.9m accumulated growth clawed back; BFL increases £2.941m → £4.281m but zero growth assumption
findings.quote: The Business Rates Reset has moved Worthing from a position of 'retained growth' to [...] of £11.9m. This [...] era (£10.6m in [...] April 2026.

findings.headline: General Fund Working Balance at 3.1% of budget, well below the council's own 6-10% policy minimum
findings.detail: The working balance is forecast to remain at £755k through 2026/27 (3.1% of budget requirement), significantly below the council's established policy of 6-10%. The council had previously held larger reserves but depleted them during earlier financial pressures. Even with planned contributions, it will take until 2027/28 to reach 6.9% adequacy.
findings.matters: Minimal reserves mean the council has almost no buffer for unexpected costs, income shortfalls, or service demands. This increases credit risk because any adverse variance forces deeper service cuts or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Current balance £755k; 3.1% of budget requirement; policy minimum 6%; target minimum £1.2m
findings.quote: The working balance is currently projected to be too low at the year end. Whilst there are [options] this reserve, these [are limited]

findings.headline: Council applying for £5m exceptional financial support to balance the budget
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget has a shortfall of £4,472k that cannot be closed through savings or council tax alone. The council is requesting £5m in exceptional financial support through a capitalisation direction. Without this government bailout, the budget cannot be balanced. The previous estimate sought £4m; the increase reflects growing pressures.
findings.matters: This signals structural insolvency: the council cannot fund its services from normal revenues and must borrow from government to stay solvent. For a lender, this is a critical credit indicator.
findings.figures: Shortfall of £4,472k; EFS requested £5m; only £4m was previously identified
findings.quote: Confirmation of the amount being asked for within the exceptional financial support framework through a capitalisation direction.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Opposition Leader Budget Speech 2026
findings.headline: Reserve provision increased from £500,000 to £950,000 while requesting emergency government support, raising questions about financial strategy
findings.detail: Reserves are increasing significantly (90% increase year-on-year) at the same time the council is requesting exceptional financial support. The opposition argues this is counter-intuitive and questions why the council is raising council tax (2.97%) to build reserves when the authority is being dissolved into a unitary in two years.
findings.matters: A lender would want to understand why reserves are being accumulated when the council claims financial distress and is requesting bailouts. This apparent contradiction raises questions about reserve adequacy, financial planning coherence, or whether the council is overstating its difficulties.
findings.figures: £500,000 planned reserves (prior year) increased to £950,000 (this year); council tax rise of 2.97% generating approximately £300,000
findings.quote: Last year this council planned to put £500,000 into reserves, this year that figure has increased to £950,000.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Opposition Leader Budget Speech 2026
findings.headline: Council is selling its largest development land (West Durrington) to plug borrowing costs rather than develop affordable housing
findings.detail: Instead of partnering with a developer to build affordable homes on West Durrington, the council is selling the land to absorb the receipt into its coffers to 'offset for the next two years its cost of borrowing'. This use of capital asset sales to cover operating shortfalls is a concerning signal of cash flow pressure.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts from asset sales to cover borrowing costs indicates the council cannot cover these costs from operating revenues. This suggests structural budget problems rather than temporary pressures, particularly given the council is interim before unitary authority merger.
findings.figures: West Durrington described as 'the largest piece of as yet unused development land'
findings.quote: This council is the owner of the largest piece of as yet unused development land in our town at West Durrington. Yet instead of working hand in hand with a chosen developer to build affordable homes it is intending to sell the land off to a private developer and simply absorb that massive multi million pound financial receipt into the council's coffers to offset for the next two years its cost of borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix C - Opposition Leader Budget Speech 2026
findings.headline: Exceptional financial support need jumped from £4m to £5m within months, indicating poor financial forecasting or control
findings.detail: The council requested £4m in exceptional financial support earlier in the financial year but within 'a few short months' acknowledged it had miscalculated and now needs £5m - a 25% increase. This suggests either serious forecasting weakness or rapidly deteriorating finances.
findings.matters: For a lender, a reforecast of this magnitude in such a short timeframe is a critical governance and financial control red flag. It indicates either incompetence in financial management or that the underlying financial position is worsening faster than anticipated.
findings.figures: £4m reforecast to £5m exceptional financial support
findings.quote: yet we still have a council that only earlier this financial year was saying it couldn't make the books balance and would be going to the Government cap in hand and asking for £4m in exceptional financial support and now just a few short months later saying that it got its numbers wrong and it needs 25% more than that sum, in fact it is going to the government cap in hand to ask for £5m in exceptional financial support.
